ety.text: The noun is derived from Middle English snaw, snou, snow (“snow; accumulation of snow; snowfall; snowstorm; whiteness”), from Old English snāw (“snow”), from Proto-West Germanic *snaiw (“snow”), from Proto-Germanic *snaiwaz (“snow”), from Proto-Indo-European *snóygʷʰos (“snow”), from *sneygʷʰ- (“to snow”). The verb is derived from Middle English snouen (“to snow; (figurative) to shower”), from snou, snow (noun) (see above) + -en (suffix forming the infinitive of verbs). Displaced Old English snīwan, whence English snew (obsolete).

Borrowed from Dutch snauw, snaauw, or Low German snau; further etymology uncertain, possibly from Low German snau (“beak”), related to Middle Low German snute (“snout”) (whence English snout), from Proto-West Germanic *snūt (“snout”), from Proto-Germanic *snūtaz (“snout”), possibly imitative.

senses.d: The partly frozen, crystalline state of water that falls from the atmosphere as precipitation in flakes; also, the falling of such flakes; and the accumulation of them on the ground or on objects as a white layer.
ex: Snow is white, / And lieth in the dike. And every man lets it lye.
Hovv, by the fineſt art, the native robe / To vveave; hovv, vvhite as hyperborean ſnovv, / To form the lucid lavvn; […]

senses.d: An instance of the falling of snow (etymology 1, noun sense 1); a snowfall; also, a snowstorm.
ex: We have had several heavy snows this year.
At Chriſtmas I no more deſire a Roſe, / Then vviſh a Snovv in Mayes nevv fangled ſhovves: / But like of each thing that in ſeaſon grovves.

senses.d: A period of time when snow falls; a winter.
An accumulation or spread of snow.
ex: [I]t well may happen yonder, where the far snows blanch / Mute Mont Blanc, that who stands near them sees and hears an avalanche,— […]

senses.d: A dish or component of a dish resembling snow, especially one made by whipping egg whites until creamy.
ex: apple snow    lemon snow

senses.d: The white color of snow.
ex: The daughters of the land were beautiful, with blue eyes and fair hair, and bosoms of snow, […]

senses.d: Clusters of white flowers.
The moving pattern of random dots seen on a radar or television screen, etc., when no transmission signal is being received or when there is interference.
ex: Near-synonym: static

senses.d: Sea foam; sea spray.
Also in the plural: white hair on an (older) person's head.
Preceded by the dummy subject it: to have snow (noun etymology 1, noun sense 1) fall from the atmosphere.
ex: It is snowing.    It started to snow.
In wynter whan it ſnoweth it is good ſyttynge by a good fyre: […]

senses.d: Of a thing: to fall like snow.
ex: Time on this Head has ſnovv’d, yet ſtill ’tis borne / Aloft; nor thinks but on another’s Grave.

senses.d: To cause (something) to fall like snow.
ex: Ride ten thouſand daies and nights, / Till age ſnovv vvhite haires on thee, […]
Let the skie raine Potatoes: let it thunder, to the tune of Greene-ſleeues, haile-kiſſing Comfits, and ſnovv Eringoes: […]

senses.d: To cover or scatter (a place or thing) with, or as if with, snow.
To cause (hair) to turn white; also, to cause (someone) to have white hair.
To convince or hoodwink (someone), especially by presenting confusing information or through flattery.
ex: She'll expose you / When she snows you / 'Cause she knows you

senses.d: To bluff (an opponent) in draw poker by playing a hand which has no value, or by refusing to draw any cards.
To cause (someone) to be under the effect of a drug; to dope, to drug.
ex: She looked snowed, weaved around funny, didn't seem to know much what was going on.

senses.d: Done because the alternate outcome is very unlikely to pass.
A square-rigged sailing vessel similar to a brig formerly used as a warship, with a foremast, a mainmast, and a trysail mast immediately abaft (behind) the mainmast.
ex: An ESTIMATE made of the Annual Expence of a Snow of 120 Tons, and 48 Men (Officers included) Mounting 12 Carriage Guns, beſides Swivels.

ety.text: From Middle French nege, naige (14th c.), deverbal from neiger (“to snow”). Displaced related Old French noif, from Latin nix, nivem.
Inherited from Latin nivem, from Proto-Italic *sniks, from Proto-Indo-European *snígʷʰs. Compare Portuguese neve, Spanish nieve.
Inherited from Old Spanish nieve, from Vulgar Latin *nĕvem, alteration of Latin nivem.
From Old Galician-Portuguese neve, from Vulgar Latin *nĕvem, alteration of Latin nivem.
From nevic(are) (“to snow”) + -ata (verbal noun suffix).

Inherited from Middle French neiger, from Old French negier, from Vulgar Latin *nivicāre, a verb based on Latin nivem (“snow”, noun). Compare Italian nevicare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nivicāre, a verb based on Latin nivem (“snow”, noun). By surface analysis, neve + -icare. Cognate with Sicilian nivicari.
